newsitem.title: USA: Dole says family leave measure government intrusion.
newsitem.headline: Dole says family leave measure government intrusion.

text.p: Republican presidential candidate Bob Dole on Saturday criticised a federal law letting workers take unpaid leave to care for a new child or sick family member, as he preached a message of lower taxes and less government in this key state.
At a question-and-answer session with small business people Dole, who has had trouble attracting female voters, criticised the act as unwarranted government intrusion.

President Bill Clinton calls the law one of his key achievements and plans to send legislation to Congress to expand the act as well as allow workers to trade overtime to compensatory time to meet family obligations. He has called the law one of his top achievements.

"My view is why should the federal government be getting into family leave? It ought to be left to the employees or the state or the county and the federal government ought to be out of it," Dole said.

"I believe in compassionate leave if there is a birth or a death or there is something that happens in a family ... but I again wonder about the long arm of the government," said Dole, who has long opposed the bill.
The Clinton campaign spokesman, Joe Lockhart, said Dole's stance showed he was resistant to new ideas.
"Now once again he's resisting an idea that's helped 12 million Aericans deal with family problems and keep their jobs. Resisting new ideas is no way to move into the 21st century," he said.

A White House spokesman, Barry Toiv, said Clinton planned to introduce legislation soon that would expand the Family and Medical Leave Act to guarantee workers the right to take unpaid time off during a family medical crisis.
He said Clinton had no expectation that the legislation would be approved by Congress but rather wanted to show his support for the concept.

Dole's Pittsburgh trip was his third visit to Pennsylvania in recent weeks. Recent polls show him far behind Clinton in this state, which has 23 electoral college votes, making it a key election battleground.
Dole tried to showcase his economic plan, which calls for a 15 percent income tax cut and halving of the capital gains tax, at a carefully scripted "Listening to America" question-and-answer session.

Unlike previous such events where carefully selected audience members serve up softball questions to the candidate, Dole Saturday faced a tough question about Republican proposals for student aid reductions.
Christiane Vaflor, 20, a University of Pittsburgh senior, asked Dole about student loan provisions included in a balanced budget plan pushed by the Republican-led Congress.
Dole never directly answered the question. Instead, Sen. Rick Santorum, R-Pennsylvania, angrily denied Republicans cut student aid.

When Vaflor attempted to follow up Jim Quinn, a local talk radio host, shouted her down saying: "You want to be an entrepreneur and you can't find the resources to fund your own education?" The audience applauded.
Vaflor later told reporters that Dole should have responded. "I'm putting myself through college, I've worked two jobs every semester," she complained.
The event was held at Gamma Racquet Sports Inc. which manufactures tennis equipment. Dole called for less government regulation of business, and said his tax plan would spur the economy.
"President Clinton trusts the government, we trust the people, that's the basic issue," Dole said.

Dole had made his economic plan the centrepiece of his campaign, but recent polls have shown that many Americans do not believe Dole can meet his promise for a major tax cut and a balanced budget, and many also think the economy is performing well.
A Washington Post/ABC poll released on Friday found Clinton leading Dole 51-37 percent. A New York Times, CBS poll found Clinton up 50-35 percent.
Dole travels to a rally in Wilkes Barre later Saturday before heading back to Washington.
